cases.abstract: FlexGen addresses bulk language-model inference when weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. Offloading weights, activations, and caches across GPU, CPU, and disk permits larger batches; processing multiple batches with each loaded layer amortizes weight transfers. An analytical cost model and linear-programming search select placements and batch sizes. Without CPU computation and neglecting activation I/O, asymptotic weight transfers are within twice optimal. Group-wise 4-bit compression without retraining or calibration further reduces transfers, allowing OPT-175B to avoid disk swapping. In dummy-weight benchmarks with 512-token prompts and 32-token outputs, a 16-GB T4 with 208-GB host memory and SSD achieves 0.69 generated tokens/s, or 1.12 compressed, versus 0.01 for unquantized Accelerate and DeepSpeed. This comparison supports greater bulk throughput through weight reuse and expanded batching, not low-latency generation. Separate real-weight Lambada and WikiText tests show small quality changes with 4-bit compression and sparse value-cache loading; 3-bit compression fails to preserve accuracy, and compression can reduce throughput on smaller models. Four-GPU pipelining scales decoding superlinearly, but total generation scales sublinearly for OPT-30B and OPT-175B with 32-token outputs. The benefits therefore depend on substantial host memory and throughput-oriented workloads.
cases.notes: Cache offloading releases GPU capacity for larger batches, while layer reuse amortizes weight transfers; the throughput comparison tests the combined system, not either mechanism in isolation. Compression remains a separate contribution because it can avoid disk I/O; real-weight quality tests constrain that storage benefit. Sections 4-6 and Appendix A.2 support the argument. Tables 2-5 and 12 preserve the throughput, quality, scaling, and compression boundaries. The bound concerns asymptotic weight I/O, not measured runtime optimality.

cases.abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations define hidden states by learned continuous dynamics evaluated with an ODE solver. Rather than retaining solver operations, adjoint training reconstructs the trajectory while solving an augmented ODE backward, making memory independent of function evaluations. Solver tolerances trade numerical accuracy against computation. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, an instantaneous change-of-variables theorem makes log-density evolution depend on the dynamics' Jacobian trace rather than a transformation determinant. Because traces add, continuous normalizing flows can increase additive hidden-unit width with linear density-update cost. Toy density experiments illustrate reversible sampling and density estimation. A latent-trajectory model evaluates states at arbitrary observation times without time binning and can jointly model observation timing with a Poisson likelihood. On MNIST, 0.42% error with 0.22 million parameters versus a residual network's 0.41% with 0.60 million supports comparable classification performance with fewer parameters. On synthetic spirals with 30 irregularly sampled observations, predictive RMSE of 0.1642 versus an RNN's 0.3937 supports extrapolation beyond training observation times. Backward reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing trades additional storage for reconstruction accuracy.
cases.notes: Trajectory reconstruction explains the memory saving; trace additivity explains linear cost in additive flow width. MNIST tests parameter economy at comparable error, while the spiral RMSE tests synthetic extrapolation from irregular observations, not clinical prediction. The latent model and Poisson likelihood remain distinct co-contributions. Sections 2-5 provide these relationships and comparisons; Section 6 qualifies reconstruction. Density-matching experiments use different optimizers and iteration counts, so the toy results do not establish matched-budget superiority.
